PyTorch accumulates parameter gradients across backward calls, allowing one `zero_grad()` before all chunks and one optimizer step afterward. Accumulating graph-connected loss tensors until a final backward retains their saved activations; `retain_graph=True` also preserves graph state. For independent example chunks, immediately backpropagate each chunk’s summed loss divided by the full batch’s valid-example count. This preserves the batch mean while releasing each chunk graph. Candidate-axis chunks require a shared softmax denominator: summing separate chunk cross-entropies changes the objective. [PyTorch backward documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/generated/torch.autograd.backward.html).

A useful implementation pattern is gradient caching: compute representations without recording backbone activations, detach them into gradient-requiring leaves, obtain loss gradients with respect to those representations, then recompute backbone chunks and backpropagate the cached representation gradients. Replay dropout RNG and preserve parameters/state between passes to reproduce the intended forward computation. Accumulate all contributions, including tied item-embedding gradients, before one optimizer update. This bounds backbone activation memory; the loss computation must also be chunked to bound logits memory. [GradCache implementation](https://github.com/luyug/GradCache/blob/main/src/grad_cache/grad_cache.py).

For candidate-axis cross-entropy, Apple’s Cut Cross-Entropy provides an implementation that avoids materializing the full logits matrix. A manual equivalent needs a streaming global log-sum-exp followed by recomputation of candidate blocks using gradients `softmax(logits) − one_hot(target)`, with the original reduction scaling. Use an exact configuration when checking equivalence: Apple documents `cce_exact`, which disables gradient filtering. Expect floating-point differences from accumulation order. [Cut Cross-Entropy repository](https://github.com/apple/ml-cross-entropy).
